$comment: Hosted payloads and shared missions: spacecraft that carry more than one organisation's
mission, or that are contracted to serve a programme other than their owner's.
Every entry records a PUBLISHED statement and carries the URL that states it. Nothing here
is inferred - not from an orbit, not from a spacecraft name, not from who owns the bus.
Attachment is by NORAD catalog ID only, and every ID is stamped with the registry name it
was resolved from; tests/test_programme_participation.py re-checks all of them against the
offline registry mirror. See pipeline/programme_participation.py for why, and
docs/mission-speculation-design.md 1.6 for the boundary this stays on the right side of.
Fields: programmeId (slug, groups entries into one programme), programme, abbreviation,
programmeSummary + programmeSource (what the programme is, cited), sponsor (who the
programme belongs to), operator (who flies the spacecraft), participation (hosted-payload |
(operational | ended | unstated), note (one sentence a reader meets on the card), source +
sourceName (the citation for THIS spacecraft's participation).

GBS on UHF Follow-On.programmeSummary: A U.S. Department of Defense one-way broadcast service that pushes large volumes of imagery, video and data out to deployed forces, the way a television network broadcasts rather than the way a telephone call connects.
GBS on UHF Follow-On.sponsor: the Global Broadcast Service Joint Program, led by the U.S. Space Force
GBS on UHF Follow-On.note: These U.S. Navy ultra-high-frequency communications satellites were modified during construction to carry an additional Ka-band broadcast package for a different service run by a different part of the department; the U.S. Space Force fact sheet records that the broadcast service used payloads on two such satellites without naming which, so the site lists the three that were built with the payload and does not pick two.

additionalSources.name: U.S. Space Systems Command, Global Broadcast Service fact sheet

GBS on Wideband Global SATCOM.programmeSummary: A U.S. Department of Defense one-way broadcast service that pushes large volumes of imagery, video and data out to deployed forces, the way a television network broadcasts rather than the way a telephone call connects.
GBS on Wideband Global SATCOM.sponsor: the Global Broadcast Service Joint Program, led by the U.S. Space Force
GBS on Wideband Global SATCOM.note: There is no separate broadcast box on these spacecraft: the fact sheet records an allocation of four of the satellite's own transponders to the broadcast service, which is a different programme with its own users, its own ground sites and its own budget line.

CBSP commercial capacity.participantsNote: The programme, the contracting agency and the commercial provider are all public; which spacecraft carries the traffic at any given moment is not. This site therefore attaches the programme to no object rather than guessing at one - the arrangement is contractual, so there is nothing about the spacecraft themselves that would reveal it.
CBSP commercial capacity.programmeSummary: The U.S. Navy's programme of record for buying commercial satellite communications: the Navy owns the shipboard terminals and buys the satellite capacity as a service, so no Navy hardware flies on the spacecraft at all.
CBSP commercial capacity.sponsor: the U.S. Navy, Program Executive Office C4I (PMW/A 170)
CBSP commercial capacity.operator: commercial satellite operators under contract through the Defense Information Systems Agency
CBSP commercial capacity.note: This is the purely contractual form of a shared mission, and it is the one a satellite catalog can never show you: nothing is added to the spacecraft, nothing changes about its orbit, and its registered owner stays exactly the same.
CBSP commercial capacity.sourceName: U.S. Navy Program Executive Office C4I

additionalSources.name: Inmarsat Government, the named provider under the Navy's satellite services contract

Aireon on Iridium NEXT.programmeSummary: Air-traffic surveillance from orbit: receivers on every satellite of a commercial telephone constellation listen for the position reports aircraft already broadcast, so controllers can see aircraft over oceans and poles where there is no radar.
Aireon on Iridium NEXT.sponsor: Aireon LLC, founded by Iridium with five national air navigation service providers and wholly owned by Iridium since July 2026
Aireon on Iridium NEXT.note: Aireon states that the aircraft-tracking receivers are built into each satellite of this constellation, which is why an entire commercial telephone network doubles as air-traffic surveillance infrastructure; the original 1990s satellites of the same name never carried them, which is why this claim is attached to catalog numbers rather than to the word Iridium.

Nuclear detonation detection on GPS III.programmeSummary: A treaty-monitoring sensor set - optical, X-ray, electromagnetic-pulse and charged-particle detectors - that watches for nuclear detonations, and which flies on navigation satellites instead of on spacecraft of its own.
Nuclear detonation detection on GPS III.sponsor: the National Nuclear Security Administration, U.S. Department of Energy
Nuclear detonation detection on GPS III.note: The navigation satellite you use to find your way is also a detonation detector for a different department of government: the Department of Energy pays for the sensors and builds them at Sandia and Los Alamos, and the Space Force flies them. Sandia records a current block of eight detection systems whose last unit launched on 30 May 2025, and the site attaches the programme to exactly those eight navigation satellites - the eighth of which is the one the registry shows launching that day - rather than to the whole constellation.

additionalSources.name: U.S. Department of Energy, National Nuclear Security Administration
GPS Directorate public interface control working group briefing, 2023

EPS-R on ASBM.programmeSummary: Protected, jam-resistant U.S. military communications for the Arctic, where a satellite parked over the equator cannot be seen from the ground.
EPS-R on ASBM.note: The manufacturer describes a secure payload interface that completely isolates this payload from the rest of the satellite - one spacecraft, but the tenants cannot reach each other.

Norwegian Armed Forces X-band on ASBM.programme: Norwegian Armed Forces Arctic X-band communications
Norwegian Armed Forces X-band on ASBM.programmeSummary: Norway's own military satellite communications in the High North, carried on a spacecraft owned by a Norwegian state-owned company rather than by the armed forces.
Norwegian Armed Forces X-band on ASBM.note: Space Norway states that these two satellites host payloads for the Norwegian Armed Forces, the U.S. Space Force and a commercial operator at the same time, which is why the catalog's single owner field cannot describe them.

Viasat Ka-band on ASBM.programmeSummary: Commercial broadband for aircraft, ships and ground users at high northern latitudes, sold by a commercial operator that does not own the spacecraft carrying it.
Viasat Ka-band on ASBM.note: Space Norway describes the commercial Ka-band payload as the largest aboard the spacecraft, so the biggest tenant here is neither of the two militaries also on board.

EGNOS on commercial geostationary satell.programmeSummary: Europe's satellite-based augmentation system: it broadcasts corrections that make satellite navigation accurate and trustworthy enough for an aircraft to fly an instrument approach, and it does so from commercial television satellites rather than from spacecraft of its own.
EGNOS on commercial geostationary satell.sponsor: the European Union, through the EU Agency for the Space Programme
EGNOS on commercial geostationary satell.note: The service provider's own status page lists these two commercial spacecraft as the operational transponders carrying the augmentation signal, which is why an aircraft on approach is relying on a satellite whose day job is broadcasting television.
EGNOS on commercial geostationary satell.sourceName: the European Satellite Services Provider, EGNOS service provider

GAGAN on Indian communications satellite.programmeSummary: India's satellite-based augmentation system for civil aviation, implemented jointly by the space agency and the Airports Authority of India, and carried on communications satellites whose primary business is telecommunications.
GAGAN on Indian communications satellite.sponsor: the Airports Authority of India, jointly with ISRO
GAGAN on Indian communications satellite.note: This is the case where owner and host are the same organisation and the mission still belongs to somebody else: ISRO built and flies the spacecraft, and states that the navigation signal is available through these two, but the service exists for the civil aviation authority.

MSAS augmentation signal on QZSS geostat.programmeSummary: Japan's augmentation service for civil aviation, broadcast as an extra signal from the navigation satellites of a different programme: the spacecraft belong to the Cabinet Office, and the transport ministry produces the augmentation content they transmit.
MSAS augmentation signal on QZSS geostat.sponsor: Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism
MSAS augmentation signal on QZSS geostat.operator: the Cabinet Office, Government of Japan
MSAS augmentation signal on QZSS geostat.note: The Cabinet Office's own table shows the augmentation signal on exactly the two geostationary satellites of the constellation and on none of the four in quasi-zenith orbits, and states that the transport ministry produces the augmentation signal contents - one spacecraft, two ministries, two services.
MSAS augmentation signal on QZSS geostat.sourceName: the Cabinet Office, Government of Japan

European Commission radiation monitor on.programmeSummary: An instrument measuring electron and proton fluxes along a highly elliptical Arctic orbit, so that Europe can design future navigation satellites against a radiation environment nobody had measured there.
European Commission radiation monitor on.note: A fourth tenant on the same two spacecraft: a small scientific instrument sharing a ride with two nations' military communications and a commercial broadband payload, and measuring the very radiation belts this site draws elsewhere.

European Aviation Network on Hellas-Sat.programmeSummary: In-flight passenger connectivity over Europe, delivered by an S-band satellite payload working together with a ground network of towers.
European Aviation Network on Hellas-Sat.note: This is a condominium satellite: two operators bought one spacecraft together, one taking the S-band payload and the other more than forty Ku-band transponders, and the registry can record only one of them as the owner.

Japanese Ministry of Defense X-band on S.programme: Japanese Ministry of Defense X-band satellite communications
Japanese Ministry of Defense X-band on S.programmeSummary: Japan's military X-band satellite communications network, run for the Ministry of Defense by a private company under a long-term financing arrangement rather than by the ministry itself.
Japanese Ministry of Defense X-band on S.note: The commercial Ku- and Ka-band payload and the defence X-band payload fly on the same spacecraft, and the company operating the commercial side is also the contractor running the military network.

Australian Defence Force payload on Optu.programme: Australian Defence Force satellite communications on Optus C1
Australian Defence Force payload on Optu.programmeSummary: Australian military communications at ultra-high, X and Ka-band frequencies, bought as part of a commercial telecommunications satellite rather than as a spacecraft of its own.
Australian Defence Force payload on Optu.note: One spacecraft carries commercial television capacity in one frequency band and military communications in three others, and the commercial operator holds the prime contract for the military side.

Korean military payload on Koreasat 5.programmeSummary: South Korea's first military communications payload, flown on a shared spacecraft alongside a commercial television and telecommunications payload.
Korean military payload on Koreasat 5.sponsor: the Republic of Korea Agency for Defense Development
Korean military payload on Koreasat 5.note: The spacecraft was built as South Korea's first combined civil and military communications satellite; a drive mechanism failure in 2013 reduced its capacity, and public sources do not say what remains in service.

WGS partner funding - Australia.programmeSummary: Partner nations paid for individual satellites in a U.S.-operated military communications constellation, and in exchange use the whole constellation - so a satellite funded by one country is operated by another and serves several.
WGS partner funding - Australia.note: The manufacturer records that Australia funded this spacecraft and that the funding bought the Australian Defence Force access to the whole network - the country that paid for it is not the country that flies it.

WGS partner funding - five nations.programmeSummary: Partner nations paid for individual satellites in a U.S.-operated military communications constellation, and in exchange use the whole constellation - so a satellite funded by one country is operated by another and serves several.
WGS partner funding - five nations.sponsor: Canada, Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and New Zealand, jointly with the United States
WGS partner funding - five nations.note: The manufacturer records that five countries funded this spacecraft together with the United States, and that it also serves Australia, which paid for a different one.

CHIRP on SES-2.programmeSummary: A U.S. Air Force experiment that put a wide-field-of-view infrared sensor on a commercial communications satellite instead of a dedicated military spacecraft, to see whether missile-warning technology could be proved out that way.
CHIRP on SES-2.sponsor: the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Systems Center
CHIRP on SES-2.note: The sensor rode as a guest on a commercial telecommunications satellite and was decommissioned in December 2013 after 27 months of operation; the host spacecraft continues its own commercial mission.
CHIRP on SES-2.sourceName: the U.S. Office of Space Commerce

IRIS on Intelsat 14.programmeSummary: A U.S. Department of Defense joint capability technology demonstration that flew an internet router on board a commercial communications satellite, so that traffic could be switched in orbit rather than relayed down to a ground station and back up again.
IRIS on Intelsat 14.note: The router was the first flown on a commercial geostationary satellite; the defence demonstration concluded in 2010 and the payload passed to commercial use.

GOLD on SES-14.programme: Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk
GOLD on SES-14.programmeSummary: A NASA heliophysics mission of opportunity: an ultraviolet imaging spectrograph that maps the temperature and composition of Earth's upper atmosphere across a whole hemisphere at once, from geostationary orbit.
GOLD on SES-14.note: NASA bought a seat rather than a spacecraft: the instrument looks at Earth's upper atmosphere from a commercial telecommunications satellite whose owner also sells television and data capacity from the same orbital slot.

TEMPO on Intelsat 40e.programmeSummary: NASA's first Earth Venture instrument: an ultraviolet and visible spectrometer that measures ozone, nitrogen dioxide, formaldehyde and aerosols over North America every daylight hour.
TEMPO on Intelsat 40e.note: NASA describes the instrument as attached to the Earth-facing side of a commercial communications satellite, which carries on with its own telecommunications mission from the same orbital slot.

EDRS-A on Eutelsat 9B.programmeSummary: A European public-private partnership that catches data by laser from satellites in low Earth orbit and relays it to European ground stations in near real time, instead of the low-orbiting satellite having to wait for a ground pass.
EDRS-A on Eutelsat 9B.sponsor: the European Space Agency and Airbus Defence and Space
EDRS-A on Eutelsat 9B.note: The first relay node of the system is a laser terminal riding on a commercial television satellite; the same spacecraft broadcasts Eutelsat's own commercial payload.

LCRD on STPSat-6.programmeSummary: A NASA demonstration of two-way optical communications relay between the ground and geosynchronous orbit, and an experiment platform other agencies and companies can book time on.
LCRD on STPSat-6.operator: the U.S. Space Force Space Test Program
LCRD on STPSat-6.note: NASA states plainly that this is a hosted payload aboard a U.S. Space Force spacecraft: a host does not have to be commercial for the mission to belong to somebody other than the spacecraft's owner.

UVSC Pathfinder on STPSat-6.programmeSummary: An ultraviolet spectro-coronagraph built to study the origin of solar energetic particles - the radiation storms that follow a solar eruption.
UVSC Pathfinder on STPSat-6.sponsor: NASA and the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory
UVSC Pathfinder on STPSat-6.operator: the U.S. Space Force Space Test Program
UVSC Pathfinder on STPSat-6.note: The same spacecraft carries a second, unrelated science payload, which is why one satellite can appear under more than one programme here.
